goals: Use der, die, das and ein, eine, and spot endings that hint at the gender
Form the plural of nouns and use die in the plural
Use the accusative after verbs like haben, brauchen, kaufen and es gibt
Use possessive articles and object pronouns like mich, dich, ihn

title.t: der Tisch, die Lampe, das Bett

grammar.explain:
Every German noun has a grammatical gender: **der** (masculine), **die** (feminine) or **das** (neuter). The gender belongs to the word, not to the thing: a table is **der Tisch**, a lamp is **die Lampe**, a bed is **das Bett**. So always learn a noun together with its article.
The word for *a* / *an* follows the gender: **ein** for der- and das-nouns, **eine** for die-nouns: **ein Tisch**, **eine Lampe**, **ein Bett**. A pronoun follows the gender too: **der Tisch → er**, **die Lampe → sie**, **das Bett → es**. So **er** and **sie** can mean *it*: Wo ist die Lampe? **Sie** ist hier. In everyday speech, **der**, **die**, **das** are also used this way: Der Mantel? **Der** ist teuer.
Some clues help, but they are only tendencies. Nouns ending in **-ung**, **-heit** and **-keit** are nearly always die: **die Wohnung**, **die Gesundheit** (*health*). Most nouns ending in **-e** are die: **die Suppe**, **die Tasche** – but not all: **der Käse**, **der Name**. The small-making ending **-chen** always gives das: **das Hähnchen**, **das Mädchen** (*girl*). Days, months and seasons are der: **der Mai**, **der Sommer**. Words for men are usually der and words for women die (**der Vater**, **die Mutter**), but **das Kind**, **das Baby** and **das Mädchen** are das. In a compound noun, the last part decides: **das Zimmer → das Schlafzimmer**.
Careful: Persian has no der/die/das, and English says *it* for every thing. Don't use **es** for everything: Der Tisch ist neu. **Er** ist groß. With **das Kind** the pronoun is **es**, even for a girl: Das Kind heißt Mina. **Es** ist fünf. Many people say **sie** here, too.

examples.t: Der Tisch ist neu. Er ist sehr schön.
examples.s: The table is new. It's very nice.

grammar.explain:
German nouns have several plural endings, not just one. The good news: in the plural the article is always **die**, for der-, die- and das-nouns: **der Tisch → die Tische**, **die Lampe → die Lampen**, **das Kind → die Kinder**. **ein** has no plural: ein Apfel, but just **Äpfel**.
There are five main patterns. **-e**, often with an umlaut: der Tisch → Tische, der Stuhl → Stühle. **-n** or **-en**: die Lampe → Lampen, die Frau → Frauen, das Bett → Betten. **-er**, with an umlaut on a, o, u, au: das Kind → Kinder, der Mann → Männer, das Haus → Häuser. **-s**, mostly for words from other languages and words ending in -a, -i, -o, -y: das Sofa → Sofas, das Auto → Autos, das Baby → Babys. **No ending**, sometimes with an umlaut, mostly for der- and das-nouns ending in -er, -el, -en and for -chen: das Zimmer → Zimmer, der Apfel → Äpfel, der Vater → Väter.
Some tendencies help: most die-nouns take **-n** or **-en**, and nouns ending in **-e** or **-ung** almost always do. Many der-nouns take **-e**. But there are exceptions, like **die Mutter → die Mütter** and **die Tochter → die Töchter**, so learn every noun with its plural: **der Stuhl, die Stühle**.
Careful: In Persian you use the singular after a number (*se ketāb*), but in German you need the plural: **drei Kinder**, **zwei Zimmer**. A few words for money and measures stay singular: **zwanzig Euro**, **zwanzig Grad**. And the verb is plural too: Die Kinder **sind** hier.

grammar.explain:
In a sentence, the **subject** does the action, and the **object** is the person or thing the action goes to. In **Der Mann kauft einen Tisch**, the man is the subject (nominative) and the table is the object. The object of most verbs is in the **accusative**.
Only der-nouns change in the accusative: **der → den**, **ein → einen**, **kein → keinen**, **mein → meinen**. Die-nouns, das-nouns and plurals look the same as in the nominative: **die Lampe**, **das Bett**, **die Schuhe**. So: Ich habe **einen** Bruder, **eine** Schwester und **ein** Kind.
Many everyday verbs take the accusative: **haben**, **brauchen** (*to need*), **kaufen**, **nehmen**, **sehen**, **möchten**, **suchen**, **essen**, **trinken** – and **es gibt** (*there is*, *there are*): Es gibt **einen** Park. Because the article shows the case, the object can even come first: **Den Mantel** kaufe ich. The verb stays in position two.
Careful: **sein** never takes the accusative. After **ist** and **sind**, use the nominative: Das ist **ein** Tisch, not *einen* Tisch. Persian marks a definite object with *rā*, and English shows the object only in pronouns like *him*. In German, look at the article: when a der-noun is the object, you need **den**, **einen**, **keinen** or **meinen**.

grammar.explain:
German has two main words for *not*. **kein** means *no*, *not a* or *not any* and goes in front of a noun. **nicht** means *not* and negates everything else: a verb, an adjective, a place, a name, or a noun with **der**, **die**, **das** or **mein**.
Use **kein** when the positive sentence has **ein** or no article: Ich habe ein Auto → Ich habe **kein** Auto. Ich habe Zeit → Ich habe **keine** Zeit. **kein** has the same endings as **ein**, and in the plural it is **keine**: Wir haben **keine** Eier. In the accusative, der-nouns take **keinen**: Ich trinke **keinen** Kaffee.
Use **nicht** in all other cases: Ich komme **nicht**. Das ist **nicht** teuer. Das ist **nicht** mein Bruder. Ali wohnt **nicht** in Berlin.
Where does nicht go? In a simple sentence it often goes to the end, after the object: Ich schlafe **nicht**. Ich nehme den Mantel **nicht**. But it comes before an adjective (**nicht** kalt), before a place (**nicht** in Berlin) and before the second part of the verb: Ich kann **nicht** schwimmen. Ich stehe **nicht** auf.
Careful: Don't say *nicht ein*: it is Ich habe **kein** Auto. Persian puts the negation on the verb (*nadāram*), so Persian speakers often put nicht right before the verb. In German the verb stays in position two and nicht comes later: Ich **arbeite** heute **nicht**.

examples.t: Ich habe heute keine Zeit.
examples.s: I don't have time today.

grammar.explain:
Possessive articles say whose something is: **mein** (*my*), **dein** (*your*, informal), **sein** (*his*), **ihr** (*her*), **unser** (*our*), **euer** (*your*, plural), **ihr** (*their*) and **Ihr** (*your*, polite, with a capital I). For things, the owner's gender counts: der Tisch or das Haus → **sein**, die Stadt → **ihr**.
Two questions decide the form. First: who is the owner? That gives you the word: Ali → **sein**, Sara → **ihr**. Second: which noun comes after it? That gives you the ending, exactly like **ein**: **mein** Bruder (der), **meine** Schwester (die), **mein** Kind (das), **meine** Eltern (plural). In the accusative only der-nouns change: Ich rufe **meinen** Bruder an.
**euer** loses its second e when it gets an ending: **eure** Wohnung, **euren** Tisch. **unser** keeps it: **unsere** Wohnung, **unseren** Tisch. As a possessive, **ihr** has three meanings: *her*, *their* and, with a capital I, polite *your*: Sara und **ihr** Bruder, die Kinder und **ihre** Mutter, Wie ist **Ihr** Name?
Careful: The ending depends on the noun, not on the owner. *Ali and his mother* is **Ali und seine Mutter** (seine because of die Mutter), and *Sara and her brother* is **Sara und ihr Bruder**. In Persian, *-ash* means both *his* and *her*, so always check the owner: a man → **sein**, a woman → **ihr**.

grammar.explain:
Personal pronouns stand for a person or a thing. When the pronoun is the object of the verb, it is in the **accusative**: **Ich** sehe Ali. Ali sieht **mich**.
The forms are: ich → **mich**, du → **dich**, er → **ihn**, sie → **sie**, es → **es**, wir → **uns**, ihr → **euch**, sie → **sie**, Sie → **Sie**. In the third person only **er** changes, just like **der → den**. For things, choose the pronoun by the gender of the noun: Der Mantel ist schön. Ich nehme **ihn**. Die Tasche? Ich kaufe **sie**. Das Kleid? Ich nehme **es**. Die Schuhe? Ich nehme **sie**. In everyday speech you also hear **den**, **die**, **das** for things: Der Mantel? **Den** nehme ich.
Use these forms after verbs that take the accusative, for example **sehen**, **anrufen**, **brauchen**, **suchen**, **mögen**, **hören**, **kaufen** and **nehmen**. An object pronoun usually comes early in the sentence, before time words and before **nicht**: Ich rufe **dich** heute an. Ich sehe **ihn** nicht.
Careful: English *it* can be **ihn**, **sie** or **es**, so check the gender: Ich nehme **ihn** (der Mantel), not *es*. In Persian, *u rā* means both *him* and *her*; in German it is **ihn** for a man and **sie** for a woman. And don't mix up **mich** and **dich** with **mir** and **dir**: Wie geht es **dir**? uses another case, the dative, which comes in A2.
